messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Retail Worker
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Voss had been working the closing shift at a small grocery-and-home goods store when the disaster began, one of those chaotic, man-made incidents that made no sense even as it was happening. A man came in shouting about a dispute outside and threw a heavy object through the front entrance, sending people scattering and knocking over a display near the register. Daniel remembered the scene not as a continuous story but as a handful of brutal stills: the glass exploding across the tile, a woman crouching with her hands over her head, the hard press of another customer’s shoulder jammed against him in the rush to get away. Even now, the memory arrived with an awful clarity that felt more real than the everyday moments around him, as if those images had been burned into him while ordinary life had stayed faint and less substantial. What he hated most was the shame that came with remembering it. He had been embarrassed by how frozen he felt, by how he had failed to help more decisively, and that shame made him recoil from the memory as if it proved something ugly about him.

In the weeks after, Daniel found that certain things at work could pull him back into that night with almost no warning. If a customer stood too close at the checkout lane, leaning over the counter while he bagged items, his body tensed before his mind caught up, because the memory of being trapped in that crush of people came back through his skin. If someone behaved badly in the store — shouting at a cashier, demanding special treatment, cutting in line with a sneer — he felt a surge of anger and alarm that seemed bigger than the moment, because disorder and selfishness now carried the flavor of the disaster for him. Even the feel of a particular rough, gritty texture could jolt him: the kind of coarse material on a torn box corner or an abrasive cleaning pad would make him think, with no logic he trusted, of the debris and broken surfaces from that day. Those moments did not stay contained. They brought the whole scene rushing back in vivid fragments, and the sharper the recollection became, the more intensely he noticed the world for threats that resembled it. Daniel started scanning people’s distance from him, watching hands, shoulders, and tone, as if the next bad thing might announce itself through some small physical closeness or another person’s bad behavior.

To keep himself from being flooded, he tried hard not to think about it at all. When an image of the shattered entrance or the frightened woman flashed up, he would tell himself it had not really happened or that it had not been that bad, as if minimizing it could press the memory flat. But the more he pushed, the more the pictures returned on their own, and the more vivid they became, the more he felt he needed those same defenses again. Sometimes, after a day that had left him pinned by the memory, he would hurt himself physically just enough to interrupt the spiraling thoughts — a sharp, private pain that felt easier to bear than the shame and terror of what he could see in his mind. He came to rely on those moments of distraction when the images got too real, yet they left him more on edge afterward, more primed to notice every close-pressed stranger in the aisle and every rude customer at the counter as if they were warnings that another catastrophe was about to start. The strategies gave him momentary relief, but they also kept the event alive, bringing it back in harsher detail and tying his attention even tighter to the same triggers.

Over time, Daniel’s world narrowed around that cycle. He found himself choosing the end of the aisle with the most room, stepping back from customers, and making sure he had an escape route whenever the store got crowded. When someone brushed past him in a tight space, the memory would hit with full force; when the memory hit, he would clamp down harder, try not to think, or resort to hurting himself to break the loop. That only made the images return sharper, and with them came a need to watch for the next proximity, the next sign of misbehavior, the next coarse texture that might set it all off again. At home, his wife noticed how little he said about work and how quickly he changed the subject when she asked about the store. He had begun telling himself, especially on bad nights, that the whole incident was exaggerated or somehow unreal, but the very need to say that made it feel less convincing to him. Recently he finally sought help after a crowded afternoon shift left him shaking in the stockroom, ashamed by how close he had come to hurting himself again just to stop the images. He was coming in hoping to find a way to make the memories feel less like present-tense emergencies, and fearing that if they stayed this vivid much longer, he would keep retreating from work, from his wife, and from the life that still felt precariously close to the disaster.
